tagline: Follow the Umpqua through forest, former trading posts and elk pasture
intro: The Umpqua River Scenic Byway follows a winding valley through the Coast Range, linking Oakland with tidewater at Reedsport. Travel Oregon presents its 66 miles as a drive through timber towns, wine country and fur-trading history, with a driving time of three to five hours. Dense forests accompany the river; between Kellogg and Elkton its bends become especially pronounced, while the valley broadens near Reedsport.

Transport shaped these places before the scenic drive. Oakland was a railroad stop connecting routes to Portland and Sacramento. Downstream, Scottsburg served as a seaport for southern Oregon’s interior during the 1850s and 1860s. Mule trains left there with supplies for mining camps in the Siskiyou Mountains. The town declined after the Great Flood of 1862. Travelers also changed from a stagecoach arriving from Drain to a steamboat bound downriver for Gardiner.

Begin in Oakland’s two-block district of original brick buildings from the 1880s and 1890s, then continue through Sutherlin and northwest on OR 138 to the Umpqua. Pass Kellogg, join OR 38 at Elkton, and follow the river west through Scottsburg. Dean Creek’s elk pasture comes before the finish at US 101 in Reedsport.

moments.title: The walnut tree
moments.text: Twelve miles past Sutherlin, a 100-foot walnut tree stands on the left side of the highway. Its age is estimated at more than 250 years, and how this nonnative tree came to grow here is unknown.

moments.title: Fort Umpqua
moments.text: Elkton’s Fort Umpqua is a reproduction beside the Elkton Community Education Center. The Hudson’s Bay Company post it represents stood across the river, gathering and trading beaver pelts. The company first established Fort Umpqua in 1832 at the meeting of Calapooya Creek and the Umpqua River, then moved and rebuilt it near Elk Creek in 1836. Fire destroyed the fort in 1851; the post closed in 1854. The reproduction marks a trading history whose original buildings did not survive. The post served company fur operations along three rivers: the Umpqua, the Rogue and the Klamath.

moments.title: Dean Creek Elk Viewing Area
moments.text: Dean Creek’s elk pasture began as salt marsh. In the 1930s, the marshes were drained and freshwater irrigated the grasslands; farmers used the ground for cattle grazing. The Bureau of Land Management and Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife took over management in 1991. Roosevelt elk live here year-round, supported by abundant food and a mild winter climate. The pasture is generally visible from the road, and the site includes viewing platforms. Beyond the grassland, conifers and other hardwoods occupy the remainder of the wildlife area. An outdoor, covered interpretive center was built in 1991, the year the agencies took over management.
moments.notice: Pasture and wetlands lie beside the road; Roosevelt elk live here year-round.
